title: Morphometric and Molecular Identification of Sarcocystis Species in Slaughtered Livestock from the Sultanate of Oman
content: This study aims to investigate the occurrence of Sarcocystis in carcasses to develop safety measures and regulations. A total of 170 diaphragm muscle samples from cattle, sheep, and goats were collected at the Central Muscat Municipality Slaughterhouse for analysis. Histopathological evaluation of diaphragm sections revealed Sarcocystis spp. with a prevalence of 80% in sheep, 78% in cattle, and 54.3% in goats. Thin-walled intramuscular cysts with no host tissue inflammation were confirmed as positive cases. Based on microcyst morphometrics, S. tenella, S. moulei, and S. cruzi were identified in sheep, goats, and cattle, respectively. Host species showed significant variations in maximum transverse width and shape index ratios, whereas total cyst length remained statistically similar. Molecular characterization at the 28S rRNA locus identified three Sarcocystis species in slaughtered animals from Muscat: S. moulei and S. tenella in goats and sheep, respectively, and S. tenella and S. cruzi in cattle. PCR amplification yielded 1362 bp products confirmed by sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis grouped the isolates with related strains from GenBank, showing high genetic similarity among caprine and bovine isolates.Molecular markers such as the 18S rRNA locus have proven valuable for phylogenetic analysis of Sarcocystis spp. affecting livestock, but its conservative nature limits the differentiation of closely related species. To improve species identification, additional genetic markers, such as COX-1, which offer greater variability, are highly recommended. Access to genetic sequences in databases like GenBank enhances comparative analysis of Sarcocystis spp., across hosts. Research in Oman has shown that Sarcocystis strains in livestock do not correspond to those that affect humans, suggesting they may not cause sarcocystosis in humans. However, further studies are needed, particularly on immunocompromised patients with gastrointestinal symptoms, to explore the potential effects of these animal strains on human health.
